A process can read and write to a file.

When a process opens a file, the operating system returns a file descriptor that can be used to read from or write to the file.

A file descriptor is an integer that represents an open file.

File descriptors are stored in the process's file descriptor table, which keeps track of all open files for that process.

This becomes part of the Process Control Block (PCB) in the process's image.

When a parent process creates a child process using fork(), the child inherits copies of the parent's file descriptors.

Using a file as an intermediary for communication has several drawbacks:

  • It requires disk I/O, which is slower than memory-based communication.
  • It requires explicit synchronization to ensure that the reader and writer do not interfere with each other with the file markers.

A 'pipe' is a mechanism for sharing data between processes.

A pipe is a kernel-managed byte stream accessed through file descriptors where the programmer doesn't need to worry about the managing the file markers.

In Unix, the pipe() system call is used to create a pipe.

read() and write() system calls are used to read from and write to the pipe, respectively.

The two file descriptors are used to read and write between processes.

  • fd[0] is the read end of the pipe
  • fd[1] is the write end of the pipe

Since a child process inherits copies of the parent's file descriptors, it can use the pipe for communication with the parent.

#include <iostream>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/wait.h>

using namespace std;

int main(int argc, char* argv[])
{
    int status;

    //hold the file descriptors for an input and output stream
    int fd[2];

    //pipe returns -1 if failed
    if(pipe(fd) < 0) //error
    {
        exit(1);
    }

    //create the child, it inherits copies of the parent's file descriptors
    if(fork() == 0) //child
    {
        //buffer to hold the data
        char buffer[100];

        //close the writing end of the pipe
        //1. Prevents resource leaks (file descriptors are limited)
        //2. Allows proper EOF detection—if the write end isn't closed, `read()` will block forever waiting for more data
        close(fd[1]);

        cout<<"I am the child, waiting to read from parent..."<<endl;

        //read from the pipe
        ssize_t bytesRead = read(fd[0], buffer, sizeof(buffer) - 1);

        //makes sure that some data was read
        if (bytesRead > 0) {
            //null-terminate the buffer to make it a valid C-string
            buffer[bytesRead] = '\0';

            //print output
            cout<<"I am the child, printing the received message: "<<buffer<<endl;
        }

        close(fd[0]); //close the read end of the pipe
    }
    else //parent
    {
        //sleep(2);
        
        //synchronize the two processes, child blocks on read
        cout<<"I am the parent, sending a message to a child... "<<endl;

        close(fd[0]); //close the read end of the pipe

        //create a C-string message to send to the child
        const char message[] = "Hello World!";
        //write to the pipe
        write(fd[1], message, sizeof(message));

        wait(&status);

        cout<<"I am the parent, successful sending a message"<<endl;

        close(fd[1]); //close the write end of the pipe
    }
    return 0;
}

The key to the coordination between the parent and child processes is that the child process blocks on the read() system call until the parent process writes to the pipe.

Calls to read() and write() both return the number of bytes read or written. A return value of 0 from read() indicates EOF, while a return value of -1 indicates an error.

If all write ends are closed, read() returns 0, meaning EOF.

If we wanted two way communication, we would need to create two pipes.

#include <iostream>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/wait.h>

using namespace std;

int main(int argc, char* argv[])
{
    int status;

    //for reading and writing between two processes
    int parentToChildFd[2];
    int childToParentFd[2];

    //check for an error creating the pipes
    if(pipe(parentToChildFd) < 0 || pipe(childToParentFd) < 0) 
    {
        cout<<"Error creating a pipe"<<endl;
        exit(1);
    }

    //create an int to serve as a buffer 
    int numRead = 0;
    
    //create a child process
    if(fork() == 0) //child
    {
        //close unused pipe ends in the child process
        close(parentToChildFd[1]); //child won't write to this pipe
        close(childToParentFd[0]); //child won't read from this pipe

        //go back and forth sending and receiving data
        for(int i = 0;i < 5;i++)
        {
            //read 4 bytes from pipe and store in the buffer
            read(parentToChildFd[0], &numRead, sizeof(numRead));

            //add one to the read in value
            numRead++;

            //print out the new value
            cout<<"Child: "<<numRead<<endl;

            //write the new value back through the pipe
            write(childToParentFd[1], &numRead, sizeof(numRead));
        }

        //done, close the pipe ends used by the child process
        close(parentToChildFd[0]);
        close(childToParentFd[1]);
    }
    else //parent
    {
        //close unused pipe ends in the parent process
        close(parentToChildFd[0]); //parent won't read from this pipe
        close(childToParentFd[1]); //parent won't write to this pipe

        //go back and forth sending and receiving data
        for(int i = 0;i < 5;i++)
        {
            //print the current value
            cout<<"Parent: "<<numRead<<endl;

            //write it to the child
            write(parentToChildFd[1], &numRead, sizeof(numRead));

            //read in updated value from the child
            read(childToParentFd[0], &numRead, sizeof(numRead));

            //add one to the read in value
            numRead++;
        }
        
        //done, close the pipe ends used by the parent process
        close(parentToChildFd[1]);
        close(childToParentFd[0]);

        //wait for the child process to finish
        wait(&status);
    }
    return 0;
}

Expected output:
Parent: 0
Child: 1
Parent: 2
Child: 3
 ...

Pipe rules:

  1. fd[0] is used for reading; fd[1] is used for writing.
  2. Data written to a pipe is read in FIFO order.
  3. Reading an empty pipe blocks while a writer still exists.
  4. Reading returns 0 when all write ends are closed and the pipe is empty.
  5. Writing can block when the pipe's kernel buffer is full.
  6. After fork(), close every descriptor that a process does not use.
